title: Placer gold (USGS model 39a, placer Au-PGE)
percentile_convention: USGS: p90 is the value that 90% of deposits equal or exceed (the small end); p10 the large end

sources.citation: Orris, G.J., and Bliss, J.D., 1986, Grade and tonnage model of placer Au-PGE, in Cox, D.P., and Singer, D.A., eds., Mineral deposit models: U.S. Geological Survey Bulletin 1693, p. 261-264; with Yeend, W.E., 1986, Descriptive model of placer Au-PGE, same volume, p. 261.
Orris, G.J., and Bliss, J.D., 1985, Geologic and grade-volume data on 330 gold placer deposits: U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 85-213, 173 p.
Bliss, J.D., ed., 1992, Developments in mineral deposit modeling: U.S. Geological Survey Bulletin 2004, 168 p.

Schmidt, J.M., Light, T.D., Drew, L.J., Wilson, F.H., Miller, M.L., and Saltus, R.W., 2007, Undiscovered locatable mineral resources in the Bay Resource Management Plan Area, Alaska: A probabilistic assessment: U.S. Geological Survey Scientific Investigations Report 2007-5039, 50 p.
Singer, D.A., Berger, V.I., and Moring, B.C., 2008, Porphyry copper deposits of the world: database and grade and tonnage models, 2008: U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 2008-1155, 45 p.

tonnage_mt.where: Figure 196 ('Tonnages of placer Au-PGE deposits', n = 65), p. 263 (PDF p. 279)
tonnage_mt.note: Intercept labels printed on the figure (0.022, 1.1, 50; read at 400 dpi, unambiguous). Units: million metric tonnes of gravel, CONVERTED by the authors from cubic metres at 2.0 t/m3 ('Placer sizes were initially recorded in terms of cubic meters ... converted to metric tons ... using 2.0 metric tons per cubic meter', p. 262, PDF p. 278); divide by 2.0 to recover million m3. Grade and tonnage are 'for districts or for placer operations within one mile (1.6 km) of one another'; some tonnages were estimated from the size of workings. This 1986 model is still the USGS placer-gold model: SIR 2007-5039 (p. 28, PDF p. 36) uses it and restates the median as 1.1 Mt and 0.2 g/t. No newer USGS placer-gold grade-tonnage model was found (Bulletin 2004 has none; OFR 85-213 is the underlying data compilation without percentiles; OFR 80-799 has none for placer Au).

au_gpt.where: Figure 197A ('Precious-metal grades of placer Au-PGE deposits. A, Gold', n = 65), p. 264 (PDF p. 280)
au_gpt.note: Intercept labels printed on the figure (0.084, 0.2, 0.48). Grades were recorded in grams per cubic metre and converted to g/t at 2.0 t/m3 (p. 262), so the original g/m3 values are twice these (au_g_m3 = au_gpt x 2.0). Every deposit in the model has a gold grade (the curve starts at 1.0).

ag_gpt.where: Figure 197B ('B, Silver'), p. 264 (PDF p. 280); n = 16 from text, p. 262 (PDF p. 278)
ag_gpt.note: Only the p10 intercept (0.036 g/t) is printed. p90 and p50 are 0 by the USGS convention (unreported treated as zero) because the Ag curve starts at a proportion of about 0.26 (digitised, +/- 0.01), i.e. only about a quarter of the 65 deposits report Ag; they are implied, not printed. n_reported = 16 is the n the text gives for the Au-Ag correlation; the curve top (~0.26 = ~17/65) could mean 16 or 17 deposits. Units converted from g/m3 at 2.0 t/m3 like Au.

correlations.where: Text, p. 262 (PDF p. 278) ('Gold grade is correlated with tonnage (r = -0.35)')
correlations.note: Neither n nor significance is printed. If n = 65 (the whole model), |r| = 0.35 would exceed the two-tailed 1 % critical value of about 0.32; that is our inference, not a USGS statement.

correlations.where: Text, p. 262 (PDF p. 278) ('and with silver grade (r = 0.66, n = 16)')
correlations.note: Significance not printed (with n = 16 the two-tailed 1 % critical value is about 0.62; our inference only).

ore_density_t_m3.note: '2.0 metric tons per cubic meter--the average density of wet sand and gravel', used by the authors to convert volumes (m3) and grades (g/m3) to metric tons and g/t.

deposits_per_1e5_km2.note: No USGS deposit-density model for placer gold was found. The only related figures are tract-specific subjective estimates: SIR 2007-5039 estimated 1, 2 and 7 undiscovered placer gold deposits (90th, 50th, 10th percentiles) in tract PLACER1 of 55,350 km2, southwestern Alaska, plus 'as many as 25' smaller recreational-scale placers.

min_separation_m.note: 'In most cases, the grade and tonnage figures are for districts or for placer operations within one mile (1.6 km) of one another.' Same rule in OFR 85-213 caveat 1, p. 2 ('single deposits (placers within 1 mile of each other), districts, and individual placer workings').

sir2007_5039_restated_median_tonnage_mt.note: 'consistent with the tonnage and grade curves of Orris and Bliss (1986) (median 1.1 million metric tons, 0.2 gpt gold)'. Confirms the Figure 196/197 medians. The same paragraph says the model 'includes no Alaskan examples' and excludes mountain-front regional placers, which supplied much of Alaska's historic placer gold.

distance_from_source_km.where: Descriptive model 39a, p. 261 (PDF p. 277); Figure 195, p. 263 (PDF p. 279)
distance_from_source_km.note: No USGS source opened gives a typical transport distance from the lode. Model 39a: 'Au placers commonly derive from various Au vein-type deposits as well as porphyry copper, Cu skarn, and polymetallic replacement deposits'; 'Au nuggets have decreasing Ag content with distance from source'. See schematic_valley_section_width_km_* for the only length scale in the model, and the porphyry_cu extra assoc_placer_au_within_10km_pct_* (OFR 2008-1155 Fig. 23) for how often placer Au lies within 10 km of a porphyry.

schematic_valley_section_width_km_min.where: Figure 195 scale bar '1 to 5 km', p. 263 (PDF p. 279)
schematic_valley_section_width_km_min.note: Scale bar on a CARTOON cross-section ('three stages of heavy mineral concentrations typical of placer Au-PGE deposits': gold at the base of Tertiary gravel on the valley shoulders, at the base of Pleistocene terrace gravel, and in streambed gravel, cut into metamorphic rocks with gold-quartz veins). It indicates the order of the valley width, not a measured statistic or a transport distance.

au_fineness.where: deposit records ('FINENESS:' lines), from p. 22 (PDF p. 23) onward
au_fineness.note: No summary statistic of gold fineness is published. OFR 85-213 lists per-deposit gold (and sometimes silver) fineness where known, e.g. the first records give 850, 825 and 897 (Au); a distribution would have to be compiled from the scanned records. Model 39a (p. 261): 'Au nuggets have decreasing Ag content with distance from source'.

au_vertical_position.note: 'Highest Au values at base of gravel deposits in various gold "traps" such as natural riffles in floor of river or stream, fractured bedrock, slate, schist, phyllite, dikes, bedding planes, all structures trending transverse to direction of water flow. Au concentrations also occur within gravel deposits above clay layers that constrain the downward migration of Au particles.' Depositional environment: 'High-energy alluvial where gradients flatten and river velocities lessen, as at the inside of meanders, below rapids and falls, beneath boulders, and in vegetation mats.'

model_scope.where: Grade and tonnage model comments, p. 261-262 (PDF p. 277-278)
model_scope.note: Placers in the model are 'predominantly Quaternary in age and alluvial in nature' (descriptive model age range: Cenozoic). Excluded: desert, pre-Tertiary or Tertiary, beach, eolian, residual, eluvial and gravel-plain placers; drift-mined placers (grades too high, tonnages too small); and 'large regional placers formed at the junction of mountainous areas and an adjacent plain or valley' (dredgeable at lower grades). Cutoff grades depend on mining method (panning, sluicing, hydraulic mining, dredging, draglines) and on the gold price of the period.

placer_subtypes_indistinguishable.where: Introduction and overview, p. 2 (grade-tonnage overview paragraph)
placer_subtypes_indistinguishable.note: Bliss and others (1987) 'examined gold grades and volumes to distinguish among gold placer types but found that they could not distinguish most types of gold placers, except for the alluvial-plain and fan placers.' So one placer-gold grade-tonnage model is used for most placer types.
